### Prerequisites

In this text we will use the Indo-Arabic numerals (0, 1, 2, 3...), presented in another History Tracers text (<htcite0>). If you do not know them yet, we recommend studying that text first and then coming back here.

### Introduction

When we studied human knowledge, we saw that there are different types of intelligences (<htcite0>). As a consequence, the best approach is to present each topic in a way that matches the dominant intelligence of the person learning.

We also learned that knowledge never ends: as we learn something, we discover there is still much more to learn (<htcite1>).

These two situations lead us to an initial reflection.

Reflection 1: My strategy

Each person has their own way of learning and, throughout life, new situations always arise. Would it be possible to create strategies to grow our knowledge and better face difficulties?

### A strategy to play and to live

When we talk about strategy, we think of organized steps that help us reach a goal — and the most important goal for us, students, is to learn.

To build our own strategies and understand the steps of learning, we will start by studying a book written millennia ago and a game. Both are still in use today and serve as a foundation for learning different areas of knowledge (mathematics, biology, literature, and so on).

#### The book

Sun Tzu (孙子) was the Chinese author of the classic *The Art of War* (Bingfa - 兵法). He lived in China (Zhongguo - 中國) in the 5th century BCE, according to the Gregorian calendar (<htcite0>).

Do not be scared by the book's name! Even though "war" is in the title, we should not limit Sun Tzu's (孙子) work only to the battlefield. On the contrary: Sun Tzu (孙子) shows that battles — which we will explore here as life's challenges — are won with calculation and strategy, instead of brute force and courage. He also reinforces fundamental concepts, such as planning (<htcite1>).

#### Chess (ashtāpada, Xiangqi (象棋) and Shogi (将棋))

Almost 1,000 years after Sun Tzu's (孙子) death, a game appeared in India in which strategy and calculation are essential: ashtāpada, which would become known in part of the world as chess (<htcite2>).

In **Figure 1**, we show a chess set with the rules printed around it, held by the British Museum (<htcite3>).
Figure 1: Chess set with the rules printed around it. © Trustees of the British Museum ().

Little literature about the game survived the passage of time, but there is no doubt that its rules kept evolving as peoples adapted them: first Sassanian Persia, then the Arabs and, finally, Europe — all after importing the game from India (<htcite0>).

India was not the only place where a strategy game appeared. In the same period, this time in China (Zhongguo - 中國), Xiangqi (象棋) was created, which shares similarities with the Indian game. In *Figure 2*, we show it in the Korean version — the *changgi-set (장기판 將棋板)* — made during the Joseon dynasty (<htcite1>).
Figure 2: Korean Xiangqi game. © Trustees of the British Museum ().

There is also a third game: Shogi (将棋), played in Japan (Nippon koku or Nihon koku, 日本国). Perhaps it was influenced by one of the chess games we saw, or perhaps it arose independently. We lack data that would allow us to confirm which of the two hypotheses is correct (<htcite0>).
Figure 3: Couple playing Shogi. © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York ().

Despite the similarities of ideas between the games, there are also differences in the number of pieces and in their rules of play (<htcite0>) — and we will see those differences as we study each one of them.

The Indian, Chinese and Japanese games, as well as Sun Tzu's (孙子) text, can be used in different life scenarios. With that in mind, let's reflect:

Reflection 2: Reusing knowledge

Wars are one of the worst things that can happen to humanity: they always cause pain and suffering for every family involved.

What if, instead of using books and games made for warring, we used them to fight ignorance — about ourselves and about mathematics?

### Sun Tzu's (孙子) 5 factors

Right at the beginning of his book, Sun Tzu (孙子) mentions 5 factors that he considers constant (<htcite0>). Below, we present each one of them and adapt them to a student's life:

#### 1. The law of morale

The topic of morale is very broad. To avoid confusion, we follow the notes added to the work we are studying: for Sun Tzu (孙子), the "Law of Morale" would be the principle of harmony — that is, people in agreement with the rules.

In the translation we use, there are also notes by Wang Tzu that say:

source.text: Tzu, S., Adams, A., Griffith, S. B., & Sunzi.

text.text: • "Without constant practice, the officers will become nervous and undecided when gathered for a battle..."

Applied to our daily learning, this lesson shows us that without the constant practice of study — with tasks that help us better understand what is around us —, we can feel insecure when dealing with the unknown.

#### 2. Heaven

For Sun Tzu (孙子), this factor would mean *day and night, cold and heat, the weather and the seasons* (<htcite0>).

The understanding of the universe in Sun Tzu's (孙子) time was much more limited than ours. In general, we can read this passage as a reference to what were considered the 5 elements, the 4 seasons and other natural phenomena (<htcite1>).

For our lives, the lesson is to stay connected with nature, to understand it and to plan according to what it shows. For example, we do not wear thick clothes on a summer day, nor do we wear short clothes in the winter.

#### 3. Terrain

For Sun Tzu (孙子), "Terrain" refers to sizes (large and small), safety and danger, among other scenarios we will find in our lives.

Returning to our lives, by knowing each of these scenarios — presented here as opposite ideas —, we will be able to make better decisions. We do call the reader's attention, however, to the fact that many of the ancient understandings of two sides of the universe can be expanded to many other scenarios, as we will see ahead.

#### 4. The commander

When speaking of the commander, Sun Tzu (孙子) reinforces the qualities expected of a great leader: *wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and rigor* (<htcite2>).

These qualities are directly related to the 5 cardinal virtues of the Chinese (<htcite3>):
- Humanity or benevolence;
- Having a clear, honest and morally upright perspective, free of deceit, partiality or dishonest intentions;
- Self-respect and self-control;
- Wisdom;
- Sincerity;

The qualities expected of a commander are not limited to a single person: after all, a commander must inspire their followers. All these qualities can help us not only to guide our life in a better direction, but also to collaborate with other people and to live in harmony, even when differences exist.

#### 5. Method and discipline

When we read the description of this factor, we think of social relations: in the military area, Sun Tzu (孙子) describes for us the *organization of the army and its divisions, the gradations of ranks among officers, the maintenance of the roads...*.

This organization reminds us of our families, of workers in their workplace and, in general, of any place where more than one person works and lives together — keeping society as a whole organized.

### Chess in our lives

The fact that chess games have gone through various transformations until today, as they were adapted to new cultures, leads us to a new reflection:

Reflection 3: I have thought this way before

The Indian game went through different interpretations and modifications. Does that mean our understanding of something can change over time?

Can we see the same thing in different ways?

Even if we see the same thing in different ways, can we say that all of them are correct?

Let's answer the questions of this reflection, one by one.

#### Understanding changes over time

As our knowledge grows, what we understood before about a subject can be improved and refined. That does not mean what we knew before was wrong: in fact, the understanding was merely limited.

For example, the idea that there were only 5 elements in nature, as we saw above, was expanded: today we recognize 118 elements (<htcite0>).

#### Can we see the same thing in different ways?

As we have already learned in other History Tracers texts, humanity created different ways of counting — and all of them represent, in some way, our body. That is: they are different ways of counting, but with the same base, our body (<htcite1>).

#### Different correct ways

If it seems that there are different correct answers to the same thing, that indicates that concepts like *Terrain*, *Heaven* and *The law of morale* still need to be better understood — which avoids discomfort when dealing with some facts.

To reinforce the idea that there are different ways to obtain the same result, besides the numbers we have already seen, we show next how groups of people from different cultures were organized into pieces of the board games we have already seen.

Choose a culture to see the pieces of ancient chess:

In India arose the ashtāpada, the game that would give origin to chess. It was played with the six pieces shown below, each linked to the army of the time ().

RathaChariot
🐎AshvaHorse
🐘GajaElephant
RajaKing
🗣MantriCounselor
PadatiSoldier

Each piece had a name in Sanskrit: Ratha, the chariot; Ashva, the horse; Gaja, the elephant; Raja, the king; Mantri, the counselor; and Padati, the soldier (). Here we represent the Raja with a mukut, the Indian crown.

In the Sassanian Empire the game was adopted under the name of chatrang. The six pieces kept their link with the army, now with names in Middle Persian ().

RukhChariot
🐎AsbHorse
🐘PilElephant
ShahKing
🗣FarzinCounselor
PiadaSoldier

Each piece had a name in Middle Persian: Rukh, the chariot; Asb, the horse; Pil, the elephant; Shah, the king; Farzin, the counselor; and Piada, the soldier ().

In the Umayyad Caliphate the game was adopted under the name of shatranj, with the six pieces linked to the army and names in Arabic ().

RukhChariot
FarasHorse
FilElephant
ShahKing
FarzinCounselor
BaidaqPawn

Each piece had a name in Arabic: Rukh, the chariot; Faras, the horse; Fil, the elephant; Shah, the king; Farzin, the counselor; and Baidaq, the pawn (). Here the pieces appear in abstract shapes, without figures of living beings.

In Europe the game took on the present form of chess, with the six pieces below linked to the European medieval imagination ().

♜RookRook
♞KnightHorse
♝BishopBishop
♚KingKing
♛QueenQueen
♟PawnPawn

Each piece gets a name in English: Rook, Knight, Bishop, King, Queen and Pawn (). Here we represent the pieces with Unicode chess symbols.

In the Mutapa Empire, in Southern Africa, central power was exercised by the Mwene Mutapa, supported by a council of nine ministers and by spiritual mediums (mhondoro) ().

GanoMan with an axe
🐘NzouElephant
👤MhondoroSpiritual medium
♚Mwene MutapaKing
👥King's wivesNine ministers
MapakatwaSwordsman

Adaptation of the six pieces: Gano, the man with an axe (rook); Nzou, the elephant (like the Indian Gaja); Mhondoro, the spiritual medium; Mwene Mutapa, the king; King's wives, the nine ministers (counselors), who, despite the name, are not the king's wives; and Mapakatwa, the soldier with a sword (). Here we represent Gano and Mapakatwa with free drawings in the style of the Indian (Padati) soldier.

In the Yucatán peninsula, the Maya organized society in a hierarchy of authorities, from the lowest-ranking official to the ruler. The pieces below represent that social structure.

MacuahuitlWarrior with a macuahuitl
TopilLowest-ranking official
Ah Kuch CabHead of a district of people
BatabRuler
👥Ah KulelAssistants
NacomWar chief

Each piece represents a Maya authority: Macuahuitl, the warrior armed with the obsidian sword; Topil, the lowest-ranking official; Ah Kuch Cab, the head of a district of people; Batab, the ruler; Ah Kulel, the assistants; and Nacom, the war chief ().

In central Mexico, the Aztecs (Mexica) organized society in a hierarchy of warriors, priests and rulers. The pieces below represent that social structure.

WarriorsWarriors
CuachicquehElite troops
Sacerdotes de CalmecacReligious figures
TlatoaniKing
TlacochcálcatlGeneral
TlacatecatlGeneral

Each piece represents an Aztec authority: Warriors, the warriors; Cuachicqueh, the elite troops; Priests of the Calmecac, the religious figures; Tlatoani, the ruler; Tlacochcálcatl, one general; and Tlacatecatl, another general ().

In the Inca Empire, the army was organized in decimal units, commanded by the Sapa, the emperor, and by the Apus. The pieces below represent that military structure.

ChuncaUnits of ten
PachacaUnits of one hundred
HuarancaUnits of one thousand
HunuUnits of ten thousand
SapaKing
Apus-quipaysGenerals

The decimal units were: Chunca, ten soldiers; Pachaca, one hundred soldiers; Huaranca, one thousand soldiers; and Hunu, ten thousand soldiers. At the top were the Sapa, the emperor, and the Apus-quipays, the generals ().

It is worth pointing out that, although we have created scenarios for the Shona people (Mutapa) and for the Indigenous peoples of the Americas (*Abya Yala*) — Maya, Aztec and Inca —, there are no records of similar games among those cultures. We present these cultures in board format only to show that it would also be possible to represent them in the same game.

In a similar way, we can also represent Xiangqi (象棋) reflecting Eastern cultures. Doing so, we observe that the number of pieces and their moves are different — which reflects, among other things, the fact that, in Chinese culture, for example, emperors did not expose themselves to combat (<htcite0>). Next, we show the game as it appears in China and in Korea.

JuChariot
MaHorse
XiangElephant
ShuaiGeneral
ShiCounselor
BingSoldier
PaoCannon

Each piece gets a name in Chinese: Ju (俥), the chariot; Ma (馬), the horse; Xiang (相), the elephant; Shuai (帥), the general; Shi (仕), the counselor; Bing (兵), the soldier; and Pao (炮), the cannon (). There are seven types of pieces. The cannon, exclusive to Xiangqi, captures by jumping over another piece; while the general and the counselors remain in the palace, because, in Chinese culture, the emperor did not expose himself to combat.

ChaChariot
MaHorse
SangElephant
JangGeneral
SaCounselor
JolSoldier
PoCannon

Each piece gets a name in Korean: Cha (차), the chariot; Ma (마), the horse; Sang (상), the elephant; Jang (장), the general; Sa (사), the counselor; Jol (졸), the soldier; and Po (포), the cannon (). Here we represent the pieces of the Korean set (changgi-set) made during the Joseon dynasty, today at the British Museum.
And, finally, we show the pieces of Shogi (将棋). Notice that the pieces bring characters from cultures that also appear in other games.

ŌKing
GyokuKing
HiRook
KakuBishop
KinGold general
GinSilver general
KeiHorse
KyōLance
FuSoldier

Each piece gets a name in Japanese: Ō (王), the king; Gyoku (玉), the challenger's king; Hi (飛), the rook; Kaku (角), the bishop; Kin (金), the gold general; Gin (銀), the silver general; Kei (桂), the horse; Kyō (香), the lance; and Fu (歩), the soldier (). The king of the higher-ranking player is written 王 (Ō) and the challenger's is 玉 (Gyoku). The other pieces can be promoted upon entering the enemy zone, being turned over and changing their move.

### Conclusion

In this text we learned that the numbers we know from the previous text can be used to order constant factors of a society. We also learned that our studies can be organized and represented through different games.

One last conclusion we would like to highlight throughout the text is the non-existence of a single path — or model — to explain something. Humanity has created different models, which are improved over the years and with a better understanding of nature and of ourselves.
